utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. -- Beg your pardon. We were busy with housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, we were, Your Honour. Thank you. The first thing, Your Honour, is that -- sorry. We have still not received the list of exhibits that are going to be used with the first witness. This was ordered to be provided -- ordered by the Trial Chamber to be provided to us on Monday, was not provided on Monday. It was promised that -- by the Defence that we would receive it first thing yesterday. We did not receive it first thing yesterday. It was raised yesterday in court, and I think the indication from the Defence counsel is they did not want to be fixed to a time but it would be as soon as possible. I certainly thought it would be by now. I certainly thought it would be by yesterday. We still have not received it. So that's the first issue. And that, of course, is kind of urgent since it pertains to the first witness, who I think is going to start today. The second issue is I think Defence counsel was going to inquire with his team to find out when translations of exhibits could be provided. And then the third issue, which I don't know if it requires further discussion, but we interrupted it, had to do with the length of time that the witness after the break, Momir Bulatovic, will take. The Defence had originally indicated 10 hours, and now, as I understand it, they've now, a few days after filing that 65 ter summary, they've now doubled the time that he will take and have indicated that he'll take twice that amount of time, that he'll take 10 hours just for direct. And so they've effectively doubled the time because originally they had indicated that the time estimates were for direct, cross-examination, and Judges' questions. So originally the estimate had been 10 hours and now we've doubled that. That, of course, causes some concern about how -- what these estimates mean in the 65 ter summaries. Now, I appreciate that -- and we had the same difficulty. It's very hard to estimate the length of time a witness will take and sometimes our estimates were too high or too low. I do appreciate that. However, this is a change that occurred within a few days. So I just raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Can we start with the exhibits for today's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be introducing any exhibits through today's witness. He will just be heard. That's one. Second, as regards the time required to translate these documents, it's difficult to estimate how much time is needed. It's an acute problem that we are solving as we go along at a rate at which it is possible to translate such a number of pages. It's not prompt, Your Honour. It's difficult for me to provide any other information. I think from the amount of the material to be translated you will be able to decide whether we have done it in a timely manner or not. As for Witness Bulatovic, the Defence will review the issue carefully and if we arrive at the conclusion that there will be time enough in that week to hear another witness, we will prepare that witness or, rather, we will secure another witness first and prepare him and inform you in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I just want to note that your answers are not satisfactory. You can't keep us on a thread and keep on saying you're not able to estimate when the translations will take, you will keep track of the length of time that the witness is going to take and, if there is time, you'll introduce another witness. You've got to give realistic estimates. You've got to tell us exactly how long do you think it will take you to do the translations, how long do you think it will take you to lead your witness in the first week and have him cross-examined and questioned by the Court. We know it's not easy, but you've got to give us some estimate. Just don't say, "We will see what happens. We will keep the thing under control to the best of our ability." It just doesn't say much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry that things appear in this way, and it is not my intention to keep the Prosecution and the Chamber on such a short leash. We are ourselves on a short leash, and in giving the answers I'm giving, I'm only trying to avoid unrealistic estimates or estimates that are not grounded in anything. And when I say that I promise to do the best I can, I am bound by my word. I'm just coping with the present situation as best I can, and I hope the Trial Chamber will appreciate that. That is the only reason why we are giving the answer we are giving. There's no other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As regards the length of time it will take the witness, I want to -- because you're not able to give us any realistic estimate, the Chamber is going to pin you down to your 10-hour estimate and nothing more than that, which 10-hour estimate is still subject to a 73 ter determination by the Chamber on the 14th of August, let me just remind you. So that 10-hour estimate that you made is not the last word on the issue. It may very well change depending on the determination in terms of Rule 73 ter. I'm not sure what to say to you on the other point of translations, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'll just -- we'll just see how it goes. And I mean, obviously if -- the most important thing is that we have the exhibits as soon as possible and we're able to -- and we'll just do the best we can under the circumstances. If -- if I think that we've been somehow prejudiced in some way, I'll raise it with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That then disposes of the outstanding housekeeping issues. Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed with your opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The last topic dealt with by the Defence yesterday related to allegations in the indictment that concerned the alleged activity of the accused in the Operation Corridor and his activities, his alleged activities in the then Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence will bring witnesses and present written material to refute allegations in the indictment that the Operation Corridor was aimed at creating Greater Serbia, linking Krajina in territorial terms with Serbia, and show that this allegation in the indictment is completely untenable. We will also present documents to show that on the 26th November the agreement was concluded between General Tus of the Croatian army and the JNA, that the 110th and 120th Brigade be withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we will deny, refute the allegations that Operation Corridor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you a little bit. Can I remind you of what was mentioned to you yesterday, Mr. Milovancevic: Don't give us the full evidence. We understand that you are going to refute what is alleged to have been the intention behind Operation Corridor. We understand that. The details -- let the detail come through the witness, not through you. Okay. I would suggest that you move on to the next point that you are going to deal with, if there is any, and remember that your opening statement is really a roadmap. It's not the journey itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, but I must say that the Defence believes that it is in our interest to show the main thrusts of our case. At this stage we are starting to present our own case, and we find it very important for the Trial Chamber to understand what kind of information we have in our possession or, in other words, which key elements we will use to refute the case of the Prosecution. However, thank you for your remarks, Your Honour. In refuting this Prosecution case about the joint criminal enterprise in Croatia and Bosnia, we will use written evidence to show that even in January, 1993, the American state secretary, former State Secretary Lawrence Eagleburger unilateral -- sorry, American State Secretary Lawrence Eagleburger presented in the American Congress the unilateral recognition of independence of Bosnia as the main reason for the ensuing war. We will demonstrate that the existing evidence points to something entirely different than the Prosecution case. The Defence will also challenge the allegations in the indictment that Mr. Martic illegally, in the ways described in the indictment, equipped, armed, instigated, organised police and other units in order to allegedly expel Croat population. We will prove that this theory's in complete contradiction with evidence which is completely public and is even contained in UN Security Council Resolutions such as the one that condemns the Maslenica operation. The Defence will prove that the engagement of all forces in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had one objective and one objective only, and that is defence from armed action of Croat armed forces in those cases when UN troops were unable to prevent such action. Through our witnesses and written evidence, we will show and prove that the conduct of the participants in these events in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Croat side and the side of Bosnian Muslim authorities was accompanied by great lies and an enormous amount of deceit targeted -- targeting the international public opinion aimed at completely misrepresenting what was actually going on on the ground. The Defence will point to a document from March, 1993, from which we will be able to see that one of the most experienced American diplomats, Mr. Henry Kissinger, estimated that the international community had committed a grave error in recognising Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to show that the allegations in the indictment related to the grave suffering of civilian population are worded in such a way that they absolutely do not correspond to reality, that such suffering was caused by entirely different reasons. We will show that individual people, individual locations, and individual events have acted in a completely -- have been used by the Prosecutor to establish non-existing links and to arrive at completely erroneous conclusions. In our case, we will use a whole series of documents from 1993 to show the relationship between the forces of Republika Srpska and the Croatian population to challenge the theory of the Prosecution that the objective of the Serb forces was to expel Croats, because on four occasions, or even more often, the army of Republika Srpska accepted and received thousands and thousands of Croat civilians who were fleeing from the activities of Muslim forces. There is written and oral evidence that the Defence will present to the Trial Chamber to prove this. This completely refutes the theory that there was an intent to erase one ethnic group or even more ethnic groups from the face of the earth. We will use documents to show to the Trial Chamber that in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, despite the fact that a whole series of agreements had been concluded between Croat and Serb and Muslim forces, a great number of armed conflicts occurred between Croat and Muslim forces with which the Serb side had nothing to do, and that in the same period, in the same area, between the same protagonists, Serbs, Croats and Muslims as the local population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, throughout the period there were fierce and recurring conflicts caused by the premature recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state at a moment when the Yugoslav crisis should have been dealt with in a political manner. We will show that far from being a part of a plan to expel the local population, this was a case when three ethnic communities armed themselves and go for each other's throats in a civil war, which makes it very difficult to understand this theory about the joint criminal enterprise implemented by the Serb side. The Prosecutor himself mentioned that there were various indictments for the same period of time against Croat forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Muslim forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the very existence of these indictments goes to show that what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a horrible civil war and that in each location it is necessary to establish the real motivation, the real protagonists, and the real culprits. The Prosecutor does not do that. Instead, he isolates several locations from this all-out civil war in order to derive a theory that this was some kind of unilateral joint criminal enterprise. The Defence will show that this theory is complete fiction. We will show through witnesses and documents that throughout -- for the duration -- the entire duration of these events in Krajina, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Croatia there were several thousand representatives of United Nations on the ground. All key decisions from agreements on cease-fire, cessation of hostilities, to agreements concerning future organisation of these territories, the highest officials of both the international community and the United Nations were involved all the time, and we will show that many such agreements were travestied in order to achieve war aims, military aims, even when it was absolutely possible to implement such agreements. We will show that there was support from key international factors to attain precisely those wartime goals, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, by use of weapons. We will show that the Serbian side in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which according to the 1991 census had 581.000 population, was by far weaker. And the same was the case in Bosnia. The Serb side was much weaker than the other conflicting parties, and it was absolutely in its objective interest to have things resolved by agreement. However, every such agreement was travestied. We will show that there was an agreement reached just before the Operation Corridor on board the aircraft carrier Invincible. However, it was always the objective of the other conflicting parties to involve the international community in a military intervention. The Prosecution is saying that the accused was not cooperative, was leading his own people in a suicidal mission. The Defence will show through documents that in the beginning of February, 1994, after the report submitted by the UN Secretary-General to the effect that Croat troops are located in the neighbouring state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia publicly admitted this. Through this evidence, we will again challenge and refute the Prosecution case, which basically says that what happened in Bosnia happened because of the joint criminal enterprise implemented and pursued by the Serb side. We have already seen how that Serb side fared. The Defence will use written evidence and call witnesses to show that things were completely different to what we may conclude from the testimony of some Prosecution witnesses who said that the Serb side and this accused obstructed the implementation of all agreements. Our first witness will in fact tell us what kind of talks were held and what they focused on and point to all the concessions that the Serb side made in order to avoid what ultimately happened to them. The Defence will again present the text of the Zagreb agreement on the cessation of hostilities or, rather, cease-fire and separation of the warring sides that was concluded at the time when Mr. Martic was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Through written evidence and oral evidence, we will show what other talks were held in 1994, what happened to economic agreements [French on English channel] with his, Martic's support [French on English channel]. The Defence will show that the allegations of the Prosecution concerning the Z-4 plan as a wonderful offer that would have rescued the Serbs were completely contrary to reality. It was an enormous deception led by representatives of the Croat authorities in the interests of Croatia. We will show that all the provisions of the Z-4 plan had been offered to the Serb side two years previously by Croatia, and it was only revamped by Ambassador Galbraith in January, 1995. We will show through witnesses and evidence that Mr. Martic did not refuse the plan Z-4 because he is a thug who hates his own people and does not respect the international community, as the Prosecution would have it. He was depicted as almost retarded by Prosecution witnesses. The Defence will, however, show the real reasons why negotiations on the plan Z-4 were only put on hold until Croatia accepts an extension for the deployment of UN troops. So it was not the case that the Z-4 plan was meant to save the Serbian people and guarantee them the protection of the UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR at that moment to longer existed. Mr. Martic was insisting on securing the new mandate or an extension of the mandate of the UN forces because he thought it was the minimum protection for his people. We will show that in March, 1995, Croatia was finally forced to accept an extension of the mandate for the UN forces. However, the plan Z-4 was never offered again and everything ended in two operations, Flash and Storm, that constituted aggression. The Defence will show that all the international obligations undertaken when the UN Resolution, the Vance Plan, and the Zagreb agreement were accepted, and also all the obligations stemming from a number of negotiations were broken by Croatia. The Defence will show that the rejection of an agreement with the Serbs had only one purpose. That purpose was to implement the HDZ plan, to make Croatia a state of the Croatian people. Every agreement had to be avoided so that the issue could be settled by military means. Colonel Grujic and other Prosecution witnesses have testified to how this ended: Between 250 and 350.000 people fled from Croatia ultimately. The Defence will also point to the report to the Security Council of May, 1993, submitted by Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali showing that 251.000 people had been expelled by that date alone. The Defence will also confirm Mr. Grujic's report which says that in August, 1995, out of 50.000 Serbs who resided in Croatia at the beginning of the Yugoslav crisis, according to the official census, only 581.000 remained. The Defence will point to the real reasons why the Serbs had to organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic. Maybe there is a translation problem. You told us some figures about the Serbs who resided in Croatia at the beginning of the Yugoslav crisis, and this is 50.000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises for the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was pointing out two figures. One was from the census of 1991, according to which there were 581.000 Serbs residing in Croatia before the crisis, and the data provided by a witness, an expert witness, who said that only 50.000 Serbs remained in Croatia after Operations Flash and Storm. Only 50.000 remained. So the Serb population was expelled from Croatia during Operations Flash and Storm. When the number of Yugoslavs and ethnically undeclared are also added, this will further clarify issues, but the Defence is now pointing to a situation quite different from the one represented by the Prosecutor. The Defence will, through its witnesses, show that the attitude of the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was well-intentioned. It was cooperative, that the Serbs fulfilled all their obligations, that there are UN documents showing that heavy weapons were put under a double lock -- a double key. And there were five major offensives launched while the UN was in place as well as daily lesser incursions by the Croatian forces. We shall also provide evidence as to number of those attacks against the Serbs on the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina. The Defence will show through its witnesses that the allegations in the indictment that Operation Flash took place on the 1st of May is untrue. It only started on the 1st of May, but it ended some seven or eight days later. In our deep conviction, the Prosecution is overlooking this because they wish to separate in an artificial way the targeting of Zagreb from the attacks in Western Slavonia. The Defence will bring witnesses and present written evidence to show that the United Nations were informed on the 1st of May of the forthcoming offensive, that a Croatian armed force invited UN members to seek shelter, and then set out to massacre the population of Western Slavonia. The massacre went on for days. The Defence will bring witnesses and present written evidence to show that the firing of artillery projectiles from the Orkan system on targets in Zagreb was a legitimate attempt to deter and stop the aggression. The United Nations recognised the right to self-defence to anyone who is under attack or under threat. In Western Slavonia, it was not only Serb forces and the Serb population that were under attack; it was also the United Nations. This was an area under UN protection, and it was run over by Croatian armed forces. It was in these circumstances that the firing on Zagreb took place. The Defence will show that there are a number of written reports, written by UN officials, about the suffering of the population; that there are documents of the Croatian army showing that on the 4th of May heavy artillery fire was directed at a number of villages populated by civilians; that there was a massacre ongoing; and that the UN was doing nothing to stop this. It went on until the territory of Western Slavonia had been cleansed. The Defence will also present to the Chamber a written document from Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the UN High Representative of Human Rights who confirmed that the forces of the Croatian police and army killed Serb civilians and targeted civilian targets and facilities. Through witnesses and documents, the Defence will prove that what happened during Operation Flash and Storm on the 4th of August, 1995, and subsequently over the next few months when the entire population of the Republic of Serb Krajina was expelled and 22.000 buildings destroyed in Sector South, 22.000 Serb buildings were razed to the ground with a view of making it impossible for the Serbs ever to return. The Defence will show that this was all part of a systematic and organised joint enterprise by the Croatian military and political state leadership to eliminate the Serbs from a territory on which they had lived as citizens of Croatia and a nation within Croatia. The Defence will also submit a document showing what the attitude of the Croatian authorities was to these crimes. It will show that the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, on the 4th of June, 1995, on Croatian statehood day, decorated one of the murderers of the Zec family in Zagreb. This was an eminent Serb family, and they were murdered in 1991. Four known perpetrators arrived, took away the mother and the daughter, killed the father, raped the mother and the daughter, and threw them onto a rubbish dump. The court proceedings have still not been completed, yet Mr. Tudjman decorated one of these perpetrators, whose first and last name we will reveal to the Chamber, on the 4th of June, 1995. He also decorated the terrorist Miro Baresic who long ago murdered the Yugoslav ambassador in Sweden. By pointing to these facts, the Defence is not attempting to testify but simply to explain what material it has at its disposal and what material it will present to disprove the Prosecution thesis that the fear of the Serbs was unjustified and exaggerated. On the contrary, this fear because justified, and everything that had Serbs had been afraid of, unfortunately, happened. The Defence will show documents showing that there is a number of decisions issued by the Security Council in June, 1995, after Operation Flash on -- about the activity of the Croatian forces on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It will show that Croatia failed to respect all warnings, that by taking Glamoc and Grahovo, which are right behind Knin but on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were preparing for the final blow against Knin and the Krajina in Operation Storm. The Defence will show that none of the reasons presented by Prosecution witnesses for Operation Storm, the alleged events in the Bihac pocket, are true and correct, because Janko Bobetko, the general of the Croatian army, on the 26th of June, 1995, signed a directive for the implementation of Operation Storm which began on the 4th of August, 1995. On the 5th of December, 1994 [Realtime transcript read in error "2004"], five months before Operation Flash, he also signed a directive on the implementation of Operation Flash. We will present this document to the Chamber also and show that the excuses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but is it the 5th of December, 1994, or 2004, as the record shows 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's probably a slip I made. I was speaking of 1994. Flash was on the 1st of May, 1995, and I am pointing to evidence at the disposal of the Defence that General Bobetko on the 5th of December, 1994 - not 2004, thank you for correcting me - issued an order for the carrying out of this operation. The Defence will also present documents showing that these directives for Operation Flash also meant that the Croatian forces were at the starting positions three months prior to the operation, waiting for the signal to begin, and yet the Prosecution is presenting this all as Martic's stubbornness, the stubbornness of Martic who refused to cooperate with the UN. The only thing Martic was afraid of, however, was that what happened would actually happen, and he was trying to prevent it by doing everything he possibly could in line with all moral and ethical norms. The Defence will also show through documents that on the 30th of July, 1995, Mr. Akashi and Mr. Martic, in the presence of UNPROFOR Commander Janvier, signed an agreement regulating the issue of Bihac and the behaviour of the Serb side. From this it will become clear that Bihac was not a reason for Operation Storm as -- as Ambassador Galbraith testified. The Defence will present documents and call witnesses to show that Operation Storm began in the early morning hours with all-out artillery fire and that NATO provided air support from the Aviano, from the Aviano base and that the aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt soon disabled the communications of the Republic of Serb Krajina, which had a direct influence on the development of military operations and the possibilities of the Republic of Serb Krajina to defend itself, and it was under UN protection. The Defence will present a document, written evidence, that Mr. Mato Granic, who was one of the highest ranking officials of the Republic of Croatia, explained as early as on the 6th of August, 1995, that the USA advised the Croats as to how to carry out an attack on the Krajina Serbs and gave the go-ahead. We shall see whether there is any causal link between this and Ambassador Galbraith's testimony who said that he saw Mr. Tudjman several times a day. After Operation Storm in 1995, the entire Serb population was expelled from the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, which was under UN protection, through the activities of the Croatian army. Milan Martic, who was the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, became a refugee to avoid being killed. That was the reason the Serbs fled. The Prosecutor claims in his indictment that Martic continued carrying out the joint criminal enterprise even as a refugee. In another indictment against Markac, Gotovina and Cermak, as the Defence will show, the Prosecutor indicts the Croatian top military and political leadership, saying that from the 4th of August, when "Oluja" began, once Operation Storm began and all the Serbs were expelled from Croatia, there was also armed activity in November, 1995, and systematic and total destruction of the conditions for life of Serbs in that area. On the other hand, the Prosecutor in these proceedings accuses Martic that, even as a refugee, he was involved in a joint criminal enterprise. The Defence will also present evidence to show that during Operation Flash several hundred Serbs were killed, and they were all expelled. Only 800 remained on the territory of Western Slavonia, whereas there had been some 15.000 before that. The Defence will show that in Operation Storm on the 4th of August, 1995, 1.791 persons of Serb ethnicity were killed or went missing. This is not in dispute today. 1.791 people. The rest were expelled. Among these 1.791 there were 996 civilians; 449 of them women, and 11 children. The Defence will show that, contrary to the Prosecutor's claim that Martic was involved in a joint criminal enterprise even in 1995 when he was already a refugee, there was horrendous fighting on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the one side were joint Croatian and Muslim forces, and there are documents, witnesses, and other evidence showing that it was not only Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were participating in the fighting but also regular Croatian troops on the territory of another state, and the military offensive was supported by NATO forces with bombing which lasted from end August until almost the end of September, 1995. The aim of the airstrikes was to ensure that the Croatian and Muslim forces gain the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina which the Serb side in Bosnia and Herzegovina had agreed to hand over to them as early as 1992 in the Cutileiro Plan which we have mentioned. The Defence will show that somebody wanted war and that the activities of Mr. Martic and the activities of the Yugoslav military and the political leadership had nothing to do with this. The remaining Serb population signed an agreement on the 12th of November, 1995, about peaceful reintegration into Croatia. This was the Erdut agreement. And we will show that the Serb delegation was headed by Slobodan Milosevic in Dayton, and he is allegedly the leader of the joint criminal enterprise, but in Dayton he signed the Dayton Accord on the 21st of November, 1995, which meant the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The US president, Bill Clinton, said about Slobodan Milosevic that he played a key role in Dayton. The Prosecutor claims, however, that at that time Martic was engaged in a joint criminal enterprise with him which went on until the end of 1995. The Defence will also present UN documents showing that in Geneva on the 28th of December, 1995, it was shown that cease-fire agreements were not being respected and that Serbs were being fired on and the intention was to make it impossible for the Serb population to lead a normal life. And the Defence now comes back to what it said at the beginning of this opening statement: Written evidence will be presented to show that Mr. Stjepan Mesic, who in 1991, on the 1st of July, 1991, was elected president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia when Croatia had already declared secession, gave an interview to MTB on the 7th of November, 1991 - that's a Slovenian television station - and he is the current president of Croatia, he said that he had taken up the highest office in Belgrade as president of Yugoslavia and through the mediation of the then Yugoslav diplomacy headed by Mr. Loncar, who is a Croat, he had contacted the most influential international factors to convince them that the existence of Yugoslavia was pointless. Mr. Mesic said he wanted to convey the idea of the break-up of Yugoslavia to those who had the strongest influence on its fate; Genscher and the Pope, and that the Pope and Genscher agreed to the total break-up of the SFRY. The Prosecutor, through the conference chaired by Carrington, talks about some sort of dissolution of the state. This is not a legal term, and it does not exist in the legal vocabulary of the world. Mesic explained that the Pope and Genscher agreed to the total break-up of the SFRY, and the Defence will show documents, notes made by the American ambassador to the Holy See who testified that the Holy See took unprecedented steps to recognise Croatia and Slovenia, that it exerted pressure on a number of countries, and that visits of representatives of the Holy See in mid-1991, resulted in the conclusion that it was the Serbs who were the aggressors. The Defence wishes to show by the evidence mentioned yesterday and today that in 1990, 1991, and 1992 there was only one sovereign state, Yugoslavia, that this state was broken up by armed secession and rebellion, and that matters were quite different from what the Prosecutor claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just remind you, Mr. Milovancevic, no evidence has been led yesterday and today at all. Just remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the Defence case, the Defence will attempt to prove this case, to prove this theory. That is the Defence intention. We wish to show that the theory of a joint criminal enterprise is untenable, and once this theory is disproved. The entire indictment falls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but I just want you to understand that an opening statement has no evidential value. Evidence is tendered through witnesses and not through counsel. This is what we have been trying to say the whole week. You don't prove your case by -- by standing up there as counsel and talk. If you do want to take the witness stand, you take this witness stand there, make the oath, and testify. So what you have been saying over the last two days is not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. The opening statement is not the stage of the proceedings where evidence is led. I'm just pointing to the arguments on which the Defence will insist, the thrust that our case will take so that the Trial Chamber should be able to decide if certain witnesses were relevant or not. And in the opening statement, we choose which things we will emphasise. It was our belief that the Trial Chamber should understand the direction of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was commenting on your statement at line 21, page 20, where you say: "The Defence wishes to show by the evidence mentioned yesterday and today ..." I'm just saying what you are saying has no evidential value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless it is confirmed by a witness, understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I meant to say. Maybe I did not choose my words properly. I was trying to say that through the evidence we lead, we will try to prove our case. Of course this is not evidence that I have been presenting so far. That's not the way I wanted to be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, may I add some other issue. I think you cannot take it for granted that -- that what you are showing to us, this thrust of your case, as you said, will then make clear what is being relevant or not. Then during the evidence you are then tendering, we will then still be in a position to decide about relevance. It's independent, I think, from your own --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree completely. I agree completely, Your Honour. And I appreciate what you said. The Defence will try to show through evidence that certain things are the way we think they are and it is up to the Trial Chamber to accept or refuse such evidence. To gain time, we will not go into details now in the opening statement as to how we will deal with specific charges, specific counts in the indictment, with specific dates and specific locations, because that will be the subject of our examination of every particular witness. That will follow. I would conclude my opening statement by reiterating the position of the Defence; namely, that we expect we will be able to demonstrate that the conduct of Mr. Martic had absolutely nothing to do with any joint criminal enterprise, that the joint criminal enterprise itself is a fiction that the Prosecutor has not been able to prove, that all this is about something entirely different. I have concluded my opening statement, and our first witness will be Mr. Slobodan Jarcevic, and by your leave, maybe we could take a break now, or do you prefer to bring the witness in first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I crave your indulgence, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Call your witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I remember correctly, I believe the Trial Chamber should first remind the witness of his obligations, or maybe you prefer to do that after hearing his personal details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, may you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jarcevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence will now begin your examination-in-chief. Before we start, I have a request to make of you. Since we both speak the same language and do not need the services of interpreters, I would appreciate it if you would make a very slight pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters are able to follow.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I will abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So will I. And I have one more thing to ask you. If you can, try to avoid overlapping in conversation so that things are clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Jarcevic, born in 1942 in Gornja Ravno village in Bosnia. I was born during the Second World War, and maybe it is curious to mention that I am one of the few surviving babies from my area. The Croatian army killed many --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have to interrupt you but it was important to get the personal details. First, you were born in 1942. You were born in Ravno.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Gornja Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that Kupres municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity and religion, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb of the Christian Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, I seem to be experiencing problems with my audio system on the volume. It seems to have a slight glitch on it where the voice is breaking up in the translation. It doesn't normally happen. I don't quite know what it is. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Your patience, please. Thank you. Thank you. Yes. This seems to be much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it necessary to come back to one of the questions or can we just continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your education and your career.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary school of economics in Kikinda, the political sciences school of the University of Belgrade, and I worked as a diplomat in Yugoslavia from 1970 until 2002. I am also a member of the Association of Authors in Serbia, and I authored a number of articles about the history of Balkans and the situation of our peoples between great powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you worked in the Foreign Ministry. Can you enumerate some countries where you served as a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I served for a longer or shorter time in Zambia, Romania, Kuwait, Greece, India, and my last posting was in Belorussia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is now a convenient time for a break, a quarter past 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. Thank you very much. We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, we will now continue our examination-in-chief. Before the break, you mentioned several countries in which you served as a diplomat, and you said the last one was Belorussia. When did you serve in Belorussia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. Sorry about this. Your last posting as a diplomat of Yugoslavia was Belorussia. When did you return from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? 2001 or a bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: You heard me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to be engaged as the foreign minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? In fact, were you a foreign minister of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the foreign minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from -- from October, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear which year. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the year. The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the foreign minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from October, 1992, to April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While we are talking about the posts you occupied, after April, 1994, did you occupy any other post in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was replaced as foreign minister by Dr. Milan Babic, and then the president of the RSK, Mr. Milan Martic, asked me to stay on in his cabinet and to assist him with foreign affairs, to handle the contacts with the corps diplomatic in Belgrade, with representatives of Member States of the United Nations, with the European Community, and other international organisations. I accepted that, and I remained as assistant for foreign affairs to President Martic until the 26th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've mentioned that from October, 1992, you were the foreign minister of RSK, can you tell us where you were just before you became foreign minister and how did it come about that you were appointed as foreign minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber wishes me to, I can explain the circumstances under which I went to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In 1992, I was employed in the Federal Secretariat for Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In other words, the Foreign Ministry. In the meantime, the unfortunate propaganda against Serbs was organised in a campaign, and I realised as a native of Bosnia and Herzegovina that we were facing the same danger as in 1941, and I joined the Association of Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina in Serbia. Years 1991 and 1992 brought with them precisely the things that I feared. When I went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was with a group of my countrymen who had survived the massacres that took place in the vicinity of Livno -- Lim and Duvno in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I called up the ambassador, and I told him that I have information that the Muslims were preparing a massacre by biological weapons of Bosnian Serbs. And let me remind the Trial Chamber that 70 per cent and 80 per cent of Serbs were killed in those towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He promised that he would call up the minister of foreign affairs of Portugal and that through their ambassador in Zagreb they would contact the Croatian president, Tudjman. And there are many witnesses who can testify that people in Duvno were lined up for execution and the knife was at the ready, just as in 1941. Then a jeep of the Croatian army rushed in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness mentioned he called up the ambassador. Ambassador of which country, to which country, and what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain. You said you heard -- in fact, according to your information, Serbs in that area were in danger, and you called the ambassador of which country and where did he intercede? First of all, tell me, in which period of time did this happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was 1992, the beginning of 1992. I was in Belgrade. As I said, there was an Association of Bosnian Serbs in Serbia, and I called up the ambassador of Portugal because that year Portugal was chairman of the European Community. It's a very important function in the European Community to this day. And I am sorry that I forgot the name of the ambassador, but it's easy to find out. It is verifiable who represented Portugal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in which country?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was then in the process of breaking up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Portuguese ambassador managed in Livno, which had a large Serb population, to bring a delegation of the Red Cross from Switzerland, and they made sure that nothing happened to the Serbs, and Serbs managed to leave the town in peace. The third action that I initiated in the Association of Bosnian Serbs in Serbia was linked to the town of Kupres, where I was born. We transferred the majority of civilians from Kupres to Belgrade and Vojvodina because we had information that Croatian units would attack that municipality because the Serb party had won the multi-party elections in that municipality and Serbs were in power there. This is a plateau whose lowest point is 1.200 metres, and it was a dominant feature in that area, and we knew that the Croats would certainly like to take over that town. It is very fortunate that we pulled the civilians out so that the losses were much lower when the regular Croatian army from Croatia attacked this territory. This territory was attacked when it was still part of Yugoslavia, on the 3rd of April, 1992. These were three actions that I handled. And my friends told about it. Mr. Zecevic, the Prime Minister of Krajina. At the time I didn't know this Mr. Zecevic, I didn't know Mr. Martic, and I didn't know anybody in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I was nominated for that job because of my contribution to saving the Serbs from those three municipalities. This is how it came about that I became the foreign minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You gave us a very long answer about how you became the foreign minister. To make the record perfectly clear, can you tell us very briefly - in one sentence - who invited you to the post of minister and when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-October, 1992, I got a telephone call from the Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Zdravko Zecevic, and he asked me to meet him in Belgrade. I accepted that and I suggested that he should not engage me because I had no official position in the party, I never occupied a single high position, and I told him that I was afraid to assume the responsibility involved in the post of foreign minister. He said we would talk again. He asked me to go home and think it over and meet him again the next day. Since I come from an area that suffered a lot throughout our history, I finally accepted his proposition to become the foreign minister of RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, Mr. Jarcevic, since you came to that post in October, 1992, were you until then employed in the Foreign Ministry, the federal Foreign Ministry in Belgrade, and how was your employment then regulated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: There was an agreement according to which Yugoslavia was able to provide technical, scientific, cultural, and other assistance to other countries through an appropriate institute. I talked to my minister and asked him to use this practice which applied to mainly to non-aligned countries, when Yugoslavia assisted those countries, and it was paid for either by Yugoslavia or by the host country or by international organisations. I asked my minister that I continued to work in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and continued to be paid from Belgrade. Maybe you will find that letter that I wrote on that occasion in which I did not dare to say that I'm going to be the foreign minister. I just wrote that I was going to work in the Foreign Ministry of the RSK. When that was approved, I sent another letter, saying that in the meantime it was decided by the government of the RSK that instead of a regular civil servant I was going to be the foreign minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After this you assumed the office of minister of foreign affairs. Can you explain, when you were appointed to that post, did you automatically become a member of the cabinet of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite usual everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where your office was and if you attended cabinet meetings; and if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I reported then in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. When?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed foreign minister in the first days of November, I attended a government or cabinet session in Knin, and I submitted a report proposing that the offices of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs remain in Belgrade. I said that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would not object to this. I explained this by putting forward the fact that no United Nations member country wanted to open a representative office in Knin, not even the Red Cross or UNICEF. They didn't want to open representative offices in the Republic of Serb Krajina. I said that in Belgrade we can maintain contacts with ambassadors and other diplomatic representatives coming from 70 or 80 countries which had their offices in Belgrade. My proposal was accepted, and therefore my office remained in Belgrade whereas my deputy had an office in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you continue to be paid from Belgrade as minister of the RSK, as foreign minister of RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. As I said, there were three ways that such cadres could be paid. I was paid by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Yugoslavia, and I was paid a little extra by the government of the RSK, up to the level of assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, could you please, if possible, speak a little slower so that the interpreters can do their job.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to the interpreters. I have the impression that I'm speaking slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the last question put by His Honour Judge Moloto, you explained that you had submitted a request pursuant to legal provisions regulating technical assistance which provided for employees in state organs to go elsewhere and this was how you regulated your legal status. What about your employment in Belgrade in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs when you were appointed minister of foreign affairs of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In my response to His Honour's question, I tried to explain. This was called simply suspension or the -- my job was still in place, but I was temporarily absent from it because of technical assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this possibility available to everyone or just you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was available to all those who were employed, not just as civil servants but also in commercial enterprises, scholarly and scientific institutes, libraries, and so on. People working in these institutions were sometimes sent to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean when you were appointed minister of foreign affairs you stopped being a civil servant in the Foreign Ministry of Yugoslavia, your job there was in suspension while you were foreign minister of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was provided for by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Mr. Jarcevic, whether you attended cabinet sessions; and if so, how frequently these were held. When I say "cabinet sessions," I'm referring to the Republic of Serb Krajina. And who attended those sessions and participated in their work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I regularly attended these sessions. They were frequently held either once a week or once a fortnight. I didn't attend if there was a delegation in Belgrade. I had to meet -- if I had to meet someone from Greece or Russia or Hungary, we had meetings with the diplomatic corps, they did meet with us, but they were very careful to leave no traces in writing of any meetings with us. You asked me, Mr. Milovancevic, who attended the cabinet sessions. Well, it was only members of the cabinet and some persons who were invited, either from the economic field or local government organs or officers who had to provide briefings on the situation along the border and the threats from the Croatian army and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In late October, 1992, when you became foreign minister of RSK, did Mr. Martic hold any office in the government of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time I met and got to know Mr. Martic. He was minister of the interior, and the first time we both met representatives of the United Nations was in November when Cyrus Vance and David Owen arrived in Knin. I can tell you some of what was discussed, and this refers to Mr. Martic, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this meeting, we'll come back to it later on, but now I'd like to know the following: In what capacity did Mr. Martic attend cabinet sessions, and did he take an active part?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was minister of the interior. That's a very important ministry in any government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic also brief the cabinet on the situation, as you did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ministers participating according to the agenda. It would all depend on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient. Mr. Jarcevic, you mentioned your first meeting as foreign minister with representatives of the international community. You mentioned Mr. Owen and Mr. Vance. What was the topic discussed at that meeting? What do you recall of what was said that had to do with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: They arrived, as they did subsequently, to ask about some particulars. Sometimes they would discuss rent payments or power cuts. However, on that occasion Mr. Vance raised the issue of the Vance Plan, his plan, which envisaged the disarming of the Serb army and police. With respect to the disarming of the Serb army, he had no objections because heavy weapons were kept under lock and key by UNPROFOR and our own officers. This was the double-key system. And then he turned to Mr. Martic and said, "Why is your police force still carrying long barrels when they should only be carrying sidearms?" Minister Martic took the floor and said more or less the following: He told Mr. Vance that the police of the RSK was carrying weapons to 7 per cent and that these were standards applicable everywhere in the world and that we had not broken any rules or imperiled anyone. Then Mr. Martic reported to Vance and Owen that the Croatian army was frequently crossing the border and that every time they did that, they killed some civilians. He said that we could only fend off such criminal attacks with long weapons, long barrels. He told Mr. Vance that the police of the RSK would give up even sidearms if the United Nations could guarantee that the population of the RSK would not be imperiled by the Croatian army. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please. Could the witness slow his pace just a little, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Vance laughed. He said nothing, and that was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this conversation and your participation in the work of the cabinet, what information did you as the new foreign minister of the RSK gain at these meetings about the situation in the RSK and the UN protected areas as regards security, conditions of life, war and peace, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to gain an impression in a very brief time period. What was astonishing was the fact that the people we met did not -- or did not want to have any idea about what was happening in Yugoslavia and the former federal unit of Croatia. I found it odd that UN documents - first of all the Vance Plan and then Resolution 762 - only noted the fact that displaced persons should come back, persons displaced from the RSK, and that nothing was said about the Serbs expelled from Croatian towns, and there were many more of these than there had been Croats in the Krajina. So I took it upon myself to inform the United Nations, its Member States, and international organisations that all the evil began when the Croatian parliament and the Croatian government put the Serbs outside the law. Slovenia had done this before. And I was very surprised that the world knew nothing about this. It was identical to what the Nazis had done to the Jews and the Gypsies, the Roma. If you're interested, I can give you two or three examples of the way that Serbs were put outside the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you mentioned the problem of the return of displaced persons and refugees. You also mentioned the Vance Plan. In view of the provision of the Vance Plan envisaging the return of displaced persons and refugees, did you discuss this with anyone from the international community? Can you tell us when and where this happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I often met with representatives of the UN, especially the chief of the civilian service, Mr. Thornberry, who is an Irishman from Great Britain, and who always avoided mentioning the fact that the largest number of expelled persons came from Croatian towns. When I asked General Nambiar, who came from India, just before his return to his homeland, he was very uncomfortable. He was silent. And as I testified in Mr. Milosevic's trial, he said the most detailed facts about expulsions of Serbs are with the Security Council but, until further notice, they have been filed away and are not to be used in operations and the work of UN civil servants. I was surprised by this, and to this very day we still don't know the reasons for this course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the expelled Serbs you are mentioning and the obligation to bring back the displaced Croats, did you point to any figures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The most interesting conversation I had about this was with General Wahlgren. I've forgotten his first name. He was a Norwegian general, and with him I raised this issue in March, 1993, when we were in Geneva to negotiate with the Croats. He was surprised by my question and said, "Mr. Jarcevic, it's impossible that UN documents do not mention the expulsion of Serbs from Croatian towns." He asked his assistant to bring him the Vance Plan, Resolution 762, and some internal documents, and I didn't know what these are, and he looked at them for a long time and said, "You are quite right. There is no mention of Croats expelling Serbs from the towns. I will raise this issue." I don't know what he did, but on the 15th of May, 1993, at the Security Council, Boutros Boutros-Ghali submitted a report and said that Serbs had been expelled from the towns outside the territory of the RSK only to Yugoslavia and only to the Krajina and that there were 251.000 of these. This is a horrendous figure because there had been 179.000 Croats living in the Krajina, but this expulsion of Serbs referred only to those who had found refuge in the Krajina and Yugoslavia. 150.000 Serbs were not mentioned. Those had fled overseas and abroad. As foreign minister, I immediately took measures to establish with the immigration authorities of these countries where there were Serbs from Croatia, but none of the UN Member States wanted to cooperate with us. The Security Council did not want to respond to my letter, and the Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, did not want to respond. Now, let me tell you how we got this information that 400.000 Serbs had been expelled. In 1993, the Croatian ambassador in New York, Mario Nobilo, informed the Security Council that in 1991, outside the Krajina there had been 470.000 Serbs living in Croatia. We counted on the fact that the Croats had expelled 80 per cent, which means that 400.000 were expelled. Only Germany spoke up, and Chancellor Kohl stated that all the Serbs would be sent back to Croatia who had taken refuge in Germany. We protested. The Germans gave us no written response, and we said if they had been expelled once, their property looted, their flats and houses taken away, what are they to do in Croatia now? Then Gert Ahrends came to see us. He was the vice-president of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, a German who spoke excellent Serbian, and he said that the German government would not send the Serbs back, as had been announced, but Germany bears the greatest costs in Europe for Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that on the territory of Croatia there were many Serbs who had been expelled, as you said, the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and especially Mr. Martic, did they in any way obstruct the return of displaced Croats to the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: As the foreign minister, I conveyed the conclusions and decisions of our government to international mediators, and we emphasised that all Croats were free to come back to Krajina but on the condition that Serbs were free to come back to Croatian towns. However, not a single employee of the United Nations agreed to talk to us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards your diplomatic activities, can you tell us whether during your term of office as foreign minister of the RSK there were any talks about the peaceful solution to the Serb-Croat conflict, that is the crisis between the RSK and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the position of the government of the RSK was to negotiate and to arrive at a solution by peaceful means, in the spirit of the Vance Plan, and with respect for the rights of Serbs in the RSK. We proceeded from the assumption that the statehood of Serbs in the RSK is the oldest in the Balkans. We had state attributes in the current meaning of the word in Austria from 1936. That is, under Austria from 1936. And Yugoslavia used to be a bi-national country to begin with, like Belgium is today. And we often said to international representatives, would you agree if Wallonians deprived the Flemish of their state rights and expelled them? I would like to present you with a document from the Vienna archives. It's a document in Latin about the Serbian constitution in Krajina from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, but there is a certain procedure for presenting evidence before this Tribunal, and that procedure has to be observed by both the Prosecution and the Defence. Since we did not envisage to tender this document at this moment, I would be grateful if you would refrain from asking that of the Trial Chamber and to continue answering my questioning. Regarding the position of the Serbian Krajina, am I correct in understanding that you in the government proceeded from the fact that Serbs used to be a nation-forming, state-forming people until the new constitution enacted in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were equal to Croats, and I was just mentioning that Serbs in Croatia had statehood before Serbia and before Montenegro. And I was just going to say that by the decision of the Croatian Assembly, 1990, Serbs who had had statehood for such a long time and had their own courts under Austria --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you, Witness, but we have to worry about time as well. Time is limited, and we have many other topics to cover. You mentioned that the government tried to negotiate. With whom? Can you tell us something about that? With whom, how, and on what subject?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The government did not reject a single proposal made by international mediators. We accepted all their proposals and negotiated with the Croats. I can talk about this with full knowledge, because I was mainly the person who prepared platforms for negotiations, and negotiations took place in Krajina, in Geneva, in New York for three months, then in Belgrade, and then in a place in Norway near Oslo and in Erdut in the eastern part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I can also talk about every particular round of those negotiations if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Erdut. Can we start with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I am entitled to suggest anything to you, but Erdut is just the fourth or the fifth meeting between delegations of the RSK and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it in order, then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I start answering too quickly. I apologise to the interpreters. When I became minister of foreign affairs, I heard that Thornberry - Cedric Thornberry - had proposed negotiations on a paper that the Croatian government passed in Zagreb. This document contained a proposal whereby Croatia was offering autonomy to Serbs in districts of Knin and Glina. All the other municipalities would become part of the Croatian state, only those two districts would have some sort of self-management, self-government. Of course these two districts formed one-third of RSK only and less than one-third of the population. The government of the RSK rejected that proposal even before I became foreign minister. It was impossible to accept that. After I became foreign minister, Thornberry said that the negotiations between delegations of RSK and the Croatian state would take place in February in New York. That was just after the aggression against Ravni Kotari, Peruca, and Maslenica on the 22nd of January, 1993, when Croat soldiers killed, if I'm not mistaken, around 700 men; some soldiers, some policemen, but mainly civilians. So we went to New York. The Croatian delegation arrived there headed by Slavko Degoricija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, can you tell us who organised this trip to New York? Was it Mr. Thornberry? And who was in the delegation of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Thornberry was in Belgrade, and he invited us, and we were met in New York by David Owen and Cyrus Vance. The latter two chaired the negotiations, but they were assisted also by the foreign minister of Russia, Vitaly Churkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was on the delegation of the RSK in New York?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The delegation of the RSK was led by its president, Goran Hadzic. There was also the Speaker of the Assembly -- help me with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mile Paspalj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mile Paspalj, and myself. The three of us led the delegation of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any ambiguity in the record, you mentioned President Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the president of the republic, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what transpired in New York?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That, too, is very curious, but very little known even among circles that normally follow political events inside and outside the country. The Croats offered autonomy only for two districts, and of course we couldn't accept that. That's why our negotiating positions were too far apart, which is why David Owen realised that there would be no agreement as they had conceived it, and he said that the two delegations would continue in Geneva in March, and we came back from New York without having accomplished anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly as saying that nothing was accomplished because the Croatian side offered autonomy to Serbs only in two districts, Knin and Glina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. These two districts comprise 11 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And all that happened in February, 1993. When did the negotiations continue, if they continued?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: We continued in Geneva in March. The Croats again come up with the same proposal and suggest that negotiations take place within the framework of a committee for national minorities, which is to say that they wanted to show to their own domestic public and the international community that we were just a national minority, not a nation on an equal footing with the Croats. And the negotiations passed in discussions whether we were a minority or not. And finally, we concluded together with the vice-chairman of the conference on Yugoslavia, Gert Ahrends, that we should not continue talking to the Croats as representatives of the Serb national minority. And I hope this document will be presented here when the time comes. We continued to talk as a state-forming nation in the former Croatia, we said good-bye, and met again in April and May. However, no agreement was reached on either occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you mentioned Geneva and the month of March. March of which year? And who was on the delegation of the RSK in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I said that the delegation went to New York in February, and in March we moved to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: 1993. And the delegation always consisted of the president of the republic of RSK, Goran Hadzic; president of the Assembly, Paspalj; and myself. And occasionally we would be accompanied by another minister from the government of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the basic obstacle to any real talks was your different understanding of the status of the Serb population in Croatia, different between the Croatian authorities and you, of course. Did it continue to be an obstacle? Did you ever refuse invitations from international representatives to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, we never rejected any such proposal or invitation. But it's very important to say that we always invoked the decision of Serbs from 1945 when the Congress of Serbs in Zagreb -- and that was the subject of the thesis of a professor of political science in Zagreb in 1989, two years before the war started, and the Serbs decided then, and it became part of the Croatian constitution, that Serbs would hold their territories in Croatia until Croatia continues to be a part of Yugoslavia, and when Croatia decides to leave Yugoslavia, it cannot take with it the ethnic Serb territories, that is, the territory of the RSK. And even people who worked in UN agencies realised this. That is why, after Geneva, they proceeded with a completely different kind of discussion. They pressured the Croatian side to take into account these historical facts and to recognise Serbs as a state-forming nation. So on the 15th of July, 1993, in the town of Erdut, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, there was a new round of negotiations. Reinforcements came in the form of the deputy state secretary of the US, Charles Redman, and deputy foreign minister of the Russian Federation, Vitaly Churkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said reinforcement came in the persons of these high officials. Could you tell us who was on the Serbian delegation and who was on the Croat delegation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was convened as usual from organise -- by organisers of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, and I believe by that time Mr. Stoltenberg had already replaced Mr. Cyrus Vance, and the authority of the two superpowers was supposed to be a guarantee that these negotiations would bring a step forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who was on the delegation of the RSK and who was on the delegation of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Deputy foreign ministers of Croatia and Russia said that there would be no direct talks between the two delegations but that they would attend the signing of the agreement in Erdut, and they would take it to the Croatian delegation to sign it in Zagreb. Before that, the two delegations would have to agree on the text proposed by the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia. The head of our delegation was the Prime Minister of RSK, Djordje Bjegovic, and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether some text was agreed upon, and what did it say if agreed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The text was agreed by both sides. The only condition put by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was that the Croatian signatory would be of the same rank as the signatory on our side. Since I was foreign minister and signatory of this agreement, the Croats accepted the proposal of the US deputy state secretary, and the agreement was signed by the minister for commerce of Croatia, and that was the first time the Croats made that concession. The contents of the agreement was as follows: Its main feature was that after the agreement was signed, both governments would set up commissions for cooperation in all areas. Those commissions were supposed to bring both sides to a state of two cantons, like the one that would begin to exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Dayton Accords, but first commissions were to work on reuniting transport, trade, economy, culture, education, et cetera.
