We agreed to that and we signed that agreement, and about 20 days after the signing - you can get hold of that document - Boutros Boutros-Ghali reported to the UN Security Council, saying that the Erdut agreement would lead to peace between the Serb and the Croat ethnic communities in Croatia and that we are looking to a peaceful solution to the war in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained this agreement in great detail and also explained how it came about. Was it ever implemented? What was its fate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting, the Prime Minister of the RSK, Mr. Bjegovic, organised commissions which were supposed to implement the agreement. After Boutros-Ghali's report, however, out of the blue news reached us from Zagreb that Tudjman had stated in public that he did not accept the Erdut agreement and that he considered it null and void. If I may add, the United Nations criticised neither Tudjman nor the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting in Erdut, did the representatives of Russia and America give any guarantees that the agreement would be implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, when I was signing this agreement, Churkin and Redman were standing behind me. The American said to me, "Mr. Jarcevic, the USA and Russia guarantee this agreement." What greater guarantee could you require? He also said to me and the Prime Minister, but as I was signing, he made this comment immediately after I signed: "If Croatia were to betray this agreement, as they often do, Russia and America will force them to carry it out." Churkin said, "If this happens, I will come first to Knin and then to Zagreb. The agreement will have to be implemented." When the president of Croatia, Tudjman, made this statement I sent a fax to Churkin and to the Russian embassy in Belgrade. They did not respond. I sent a fax saying I was on my way to Moscow to discuss this agreement. I did fly to Moscow, but when I entered the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, I was told that on that day Churkin had left for Brussels on business. I was received by Ivanov, the former minister of foreign affairs. I entered his office and asked what steps Russia was going to take against Croatia which had refused to comply with the agreement. Just imagine. Ivanov gave me a very short reply. He said he would not say a single word about the agreement and that he would not explain Russia's standpoint, and he gave me a dressing down, saying that the Serbs, they don't know how to live together with the Croats and the Muslims. He gave me the Russian example. He said there were 30 million Muslims living there and that they got on very well and that they also got on very well with the Chechens. All I could say was, Mr. Ivanov, you will have problems with the Chechnya. He didn't want to discuss anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in my understanding of your response that this agreement was never implemented because Tudjman rejected it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for starting too soon. In such a situation, the representatives of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia turned up again, Stoltenberg, his deputy Knut Vollebaek, who was the foreign minister of Norway, and they proposed secret talks to us. They said, "These public negotiations have not led to any result. The Norwegian government guarantees secrecy. We will travel to Norway, the Croatian delegation will arrive there, and the Croats guarantee that an agreement similar to the one in Erdut will be signed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Jarcevic. The Erdut agreement that you signed was signed on the 15th of July, 1993. You are now talking about Mr. Knut Vollebaek's initiative. When did it take place and who was in the RSK delegation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: This was in August and September. Knut Vollebaek turned up. Before the proposal for secret negotiations in Norway was made, I was in Belgrade on that day, he said that on the 7th of September, 1993, he would bring the Croatian proposal for a peaceful solution to Knin, and he was asking the Krajina government to accept it. Djordje Bjegovic responded, saying he would be waiting for him in Knin. On the 9th of March, Knut Vollebaek --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. On the 9th of September -- no, I apologise. On the 8th of September. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: 1993. Knut Vollebaek arrived from Zagreb, opened a file and started reading out the Croatian proposal of the text of the agreement. At that point in time, a Krajina officer came in and said, "An hour ago the Croatian army attacked the Medak pocket."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Serbian delegation and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Prime Minister Djordje Bjegovic asked Knut Vollebaek what was going on. The Croats were sending us a proposal and yet they had carried out an aggression on our territory. Of course Knut Vollebaek packed up his things, went back to Zagreb, and as a UN representative he did not accuse Croatia of anything. And you know what happened in the Medak pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I know, based on a report from the French General Jean Cot, who sent a copy of his report to the government of the RSK which I copied and used in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he said that 11 villages in Lika had been razed to the ground. All the civilians were captured and killed. All the animals were killed. He said that not even dogs or cats were left alive. Cats and dogs were hung from large trees or nailed to trees with large nails. I think that Agim Ceku who is now the so-called Prime Minister of Kosovo and a Croatian general, General Norac, if I'm correct, were in charge of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the casualties among the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: You know, my documentation was taken by the Serbian police from the ministry in 1996. I did have this information. I think over 80 Serbs were killed in those 11 villages. Of course, those who fled survived only owing to the fact that the Croatian troops did not find them in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion when Mr. Knut Vollebaek brought the Croatian offer from Zagreb, were you informed of the content of that proposal or did this happen before that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I never learned the contents of that proposal because Mr. Vollebaek closed the file and went back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, even after this, did negotiations continue? Were there other attempts to resolve matters peacefully?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, Knut Vollebaek offered us secret negotiations in Norway, as I mentioned, and we accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we accepted," Mr. Jarcevic, who accepted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking on behalf of the government of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When were these negotiations held and who was in the RSK delegation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The leader of the delegation was the president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, Goran Hadzic. I was the second-ranking member of the delegation, and there was also the defence minister, Admiral Rakic, the justice minister, Radomir Kuzet. That was the RSK delegation. And the interpreter was Bore Bozic, although one witness in the Milosevic trial testified about somebody quite different. It was Bore Bozic who was the interpreter, if that's important for the Court. The leader of the Croatian delegation was Hrvoje Sarinic, who was Franjo Tudjman's chef de cabinet, and he was also the chief of the state security of Croatia. This second title is important because of what was to follow during the two days of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, can you tell us when these negotiations were held in Oslo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of November, 1993, in a place 60 kilometres away from Oslo. I apologise for forgetting the name of that place, but it's in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these negotiations public or completely secret?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: They were strictly confidential and not a single journalist either in Belgrade or in Krajina or in Zagreb or in Norway ever got hold of any information that negotiations were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the proposals were and whether any agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Knut Vollebaek chaired, and he proposed a draft agreement. Both we and the Croats accepted it. And I think on the 3rd of November, at about 10.00 at night, about 2200 hours, we agreed to sign at 8.00 on the following morning. Vollebaek said on that occasion he would bring in all the foreign and local journalists from Oslo to attend the ceremony. He also said that the Norway state television would send a crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, before you describe what happened next - I apologise for interrupting you - can you tell us what the essence of the agreement was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was similar to the agreement signed in Erdut. There was supposed to be commissions pursuant to the agreement to agree on all areas such as traffic, the economy, education, and so on and so forth. They were supposed to create a two-canton system in Croatia, as happened afterwards in Bosnia. Of course, in Dayton they had these intentions in mind with regard to Croatia, but these were not successful. They were successful only later in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say a two-canton system, was the agreement that was reached that the RSK or, rather, its territory should be a canton within Croatia and that it should be one state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been one state with two cantons had these agreements been respected and had the commissions finished their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, one question, please. This proposal was made and you say that on behalf of the Serbian delegation you accepted it, and that the Croatian side also agreed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In Oslo we accepted it and agreed that it should be signed on the 4th of November at 8.00 in the morning in the presence of all journalists there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, will you just tell us the precise date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was the 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the 4th of November, 1993, in Oslo.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Next to Oslo. Some dozen kilometres away --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Some 60 kilometres away, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've forgotten the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be the convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We will come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, before the break we discussed talks in a place near Oslo in November, 1993. You explained that both the delegations of the RSK and the delegation of Croatia headed by Mr. Sarinic accepted the agreement on the cantonal structure of Croatia. Was that agreement signed at the press conference the next day, as scheduled?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add that the word "cantonal" was used nowhere in the agreement. However, in keeping with the agreement on a European level, it was the commissions that were supposed to bring about that state of affairs in which the canton of Serbs would be equal to the canton of Croats in Croatia. It was nowhere explicitly said. The commissions were supposed to do that work, and it was natural to expect that that would indeed be the outcome once the commerce, trade, and all the other areas were merged. However, what happened. Our people from Zagreb delivered to us a letter from the president of Croatia, Tudjman, at 10.30, and that letter was addressed to all heads of state of the world where he emphasises that Croats would not sign any agreements with insurgent Serbs, which meant that the draft agreement that we were supposed to sign the next day was made null and void. At the moment when we received the letter from the president of Croatia, the Croatian delegation had not received it yet, and I was in a very embarrassing situation because we were always the ones who were accused of being uncooperative, and we understood immediately that the press conference the next day would send out the news that it was the Serbs who wouldn't sign the agreement. So I had this letter in my hands that Knut Vollebaek didn't know anything about yet, and I called my office in Belgrade - it was open 24 hours a day - and I dictated to an associate of mine what to tell the news agencies. And I informed Mr. Knut Vollebaek that the agreement that the two delegations were supposed to sign the next day fell through. Of course, the Croats eventually received the letter too. I don't know if they informed Vollebaek or not, but the journalists who accompanied us on our way back did inform their public that the president of Croatia, Tudjman, cancelled the agreement. The next day, when we were supposed to sign the agreement, the head of the Croatian delegation took out of his file the letter and started reading it. Our minister of justice interrupted him and said, "Mr. Sarinic, don't read it. We have that letter." And he pulled out of his file the copy of the same letter. Sarinic was taken aback, and he said, "Where did you get that?" And our minister of justice said, "We have friends in Zagreb and we received it." It was all very astonishing. Even Knut Vollebaek was taken aback. And that morning, Mr. Vollebaek found out that news leaked from the Serbian side that everything would end exactly as Sarinic was about to announce. Sarinic then said, of course Mr. Tudjman is the president of Croatia, I can neither continue negotiations now nor can I sign the agreement. I don't know what the Croatian head of delegation said to the journalists because by that time we were already on our way to the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt? Mr. Jarcevic, you indicated that their commissions were supposed to implement the agreement but that the word "canton" was not mentioned anywhere in the agreement. What was the actual content of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can find that agreement -- you can get it from both the Prosecution and the Defence, although I have it in my archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I'm just asking you to testify. Don't refer me to the Prosecution. What, to your knowledge, was the content of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry about this misunderstanding. The agreement said that peace was to be restored between two sides. Neither the RSK nor Croatia was mentioned, because they didn't want to offend the pride of Croatia because it never wanted to recognise the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Among other things, the Erdut agreement envisaged that heavy weaponry would be under lock and key held by the United Nations force, and it already was by that time, but the Croatian heavy weaponry was also to be withdrawn to a distance of 10 kilometres away from the border of the RSK. Those were the main features of the agreement. Under that agreement, it was not possible to renew military conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This press conference that you mentioned, was it an end to attempts to reach an agreement? There were no new talks after that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I told you the reason: The president of Croatia forbade his delegation to sign that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After this, were there new subsequent attempts to reach a peaceful solution to the crisis in that area through agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe it's noteworthy that after this failure, Mr. Knut Vollebaek got angry with me and he said, "You ruined my career because you informed all the media." And I replied, "Why aren't you angry at Croatia? They refused to sign the agreement." He didn't say anything to that, but he later was the one who proposed a new round of talks, and our government again accepted his proposal, and his proposal was that the new round of talks be held in Belgrade in one of the villas owned by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at the proposal of Mr. Milosevic. It was in Dobanovci village, not far from Belgrade. We met there in December, but this would not be the last attempt to reach an agreement between Croatia and the RSK. I can tell you about the other attempts if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after this last failure in Oslo, Mr. Knut Vollebaek suggested new talks. To whom? Was it the government of the RSK, and who took part in those talks in Dobanovci in 1993 in December? Who was on the Croat delegation, and who was on your delegation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: December, 1993, is interesting, because elections were planned in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Those were the penultimate talks where that particular government of the RSK would be involved. Our head of delegation was again Goran Hadzic, and the head of the Croatian delegation was Hrvoje Sarinic, like in Norway. It was in December. I cannot recall the exact date, but it was just before the parliamentary and presidential elections in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the subject of those talks? Was any agreement reached, and did you attend?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended those talks, and I was accompanied again by the minister of justice, Radomir Kuzet. The head of our delegation was Goran Hadzic, president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Again the draft agreement was proposed by Knut Vollebaek. We accepted his wording. We had no major objections, with the proviso that we insisted that our side not be qualified as a national minority in that text, although the Croats insisted otherwise. However, the Croats gave in and, just before the signing, the head of the Croatian delegation took the floor, Mr. Sarinic, and he used that opportunity to talk about the clear demarcation line between the RSK and Croatia. Some areas that Croats considered their territory were included in the pink zone of RSK, and the Croats originally agreed with that. On the 8th of September, 1993, and 22nd January, 1993, they agreed that this area would be patrolled by RSK police and UN police in a limited number. However, now in this speech Mr. Sarinic said, "I don't agree with this demarcation line in Ravni Kotari because one orchard and one big agricultural compound cannot be in the territory of Krajina." Then somebody in our delegation said this was -- this is state owned now, but before the war it used to be the private property of Serbs. Sarinic replied, "Yes, but I did not receive authorisation from my government to cede this area to Krajina, and I have to consult my government again on this." That's how this round of talks ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sarinic [as interpreted], can you tell us as briefly as possible, what was the main thrust of that agreement? What was it that you were supposed to sign? What did you agree on in December, 1993, with the other side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: As I said in response to a question from the Trial Chamber, the main point was to make it impossible to renew military conflict, demarcation, withdrawal of heavy weaponry to a distance of 10 kilometres from our border, and the provision that even Croatian weaponry would be under the control of the United Nations. It was our major objective, and we managed to include it in all agreements, all the draft agreements up to that point. And each of those agreements envisaged that commissions would work to reunite activities in all areas in both states. Although, if I may add, this was not an end to negotiations. There followed another three meetings that took place or were avoided, if you want to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After these failed negotiations in December, when did the next round take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The next round was again suggested by Knut Vollebaek, and he added some new attributes. He said we would hold talks at the embassy of the Russian Federation in Zagreb. "Do you agree?" And we said we agreed to this proposal, like we always did before. And then on the 22nd, I think -- no, the 22nd of March, we travelled to Zagreb and we were about to sign that agreement at the Russian embassy in Zagreb when there was some disagreement about demarcation. We suspended talks and scheduled a new round for the 28th of March, again at the Russian embassy in Zagreb. Again Charles Redman and Vitaly Churkin were present, and as they put it, their presence was to put pressure on the Croatian side to finally sign the agreement and not cancel it again. That's how they explained it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just find out. This was now the 22nd and 28th of March, 1994? We're in the year 1994? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. Those were my last days in the post of foreign minister. The head of delegation there was Admiral Rakic. I was the second highest ranking member of the delegation, and General Mile Novakovic was the third highest ranking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the 22nd and the 23rd and then the 28th of March, 1993. Are you now talking about the well-known Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. The witness has not mentioned the 23rd. He mentioned 22nd and 28th, not the 23rd. 22nd and 28th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Honour. It was my error. I didn't mean to create confusion. We are operating with many dates as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So it was at the end of March, 1994. The year is important to me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the agreement was signed on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know one more thing. At that particular time, were presidential elections and parliamentary elections in the RSK already over, and who was the president of the RSK at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The president who won in the second round and defeated his rival Mr. Milan Babic was Mr. Martic. He accepted to go to Zagreb, although it was not simple for us to travel to other parts of the state that had expelled 400.000 Serbs by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the purpose of that Zagreb agreement? What were its most important parts? You mentioned separation of forces.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The greatest achievement of this agreement -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say in particular if you can mention the new attributes that you said Mr. Knut Vollebaek added to that contract, to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This agreement is the first one that was signed with the Croats and that was not reneged on or rendered null and void after being signed. Practically, it lasted until the Croatian occupation of the Republic of Serb Krajina. The most important provision was putting Croatian weapons 10 kilometres away from the border between the Krajina and Croatia, but these weapons, like Serb weapons, were to be under UN control. It also envisaged the continuation of negotiations between the two sides, which implied the work of commissions on setting up traffic, then trade, the economy, and so on. It was meant to be the final stage of what had begun in Erdut on the 15th of July, 1993. This idea of creating a state with two cantons, conditionally speaking, or two state-building ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do we need to have a short break? If -- we may proceed, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, on the 29th of March, 1994, delegations of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the Republic of Croatia met in the embassy of the Russian Federation in Zagreb and signed the agreement called the Zagreb agreement. Is that the one we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if this interests you, we managed to delete something from the text that had been inserted. That's why it was signed not on the 28th but on the 29th, because it said that it would operate based on UN Resolutions. However, through Churkin and Redman, we managed to get this sentence deleted because these Resolutions were contrary to the spirit of the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan said that there would be no pre-judging or pre-empting of a political solution, whereas many Resolutions treated Krajina as an integral part of Croatia. Therefore, the reference to the Resolutions was deleted at the insistence of Redman and Churkin, who listened to our proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with the implementation of the Zagreb agreement, was it envisioned that both sides should set up commissions at various levels to implement the Zagreb agreement? Were such commissions envisaged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they started to work, but I was no longer the minister of foreign affairs then and did not participate in their work. However, they achieved visible results, and it was thought that everything would be in good order without any use of weapons. If you recall, the road through Western Slavonia was opened up on the territory of RSK connecting the Croatian capital of Zagreb with eastern parts of the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, do you know whether the authorities of the RSK acted according to the Zagreb agreement and whether their units, artillery weapons, tank, and infantry weapons were withdrawn to a distance as envisaged by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was actually implemented, and I know that UNPROFOR officers said that they had forced the Croatian side to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned just a while ago that you were not involved in the work of these commissions because you were no longer the foreign minister. Can you tell us when you stopped holding the office of foreign minister and what post you were appointed to subsequently.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not wrong, it was in late April, 1994, when I left the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I stayed a few days to hand over to my successor, Dr. Milan Babic. When I wanted to return to my job in Yugoslavia, Milan Martic, the president, asked me to stay in his cabinet to take care of foreign affairs, to help him in his contacts with the United Nations and Member States of the UN. I informed the ministry of Yugoslavia about this by letter, and they approved my -- extending my work in the RSK, and so I was transferred to Mr. Martic's cabinet in another part of Belgrade, not where the premises of the Foreign Ministry were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your last reply, Mr. Jarcevic, you said that you informed the authorities of Yugoslavia and that they approved you should continue working in the Krajina, but when you started your testimony today, you explained that you were simply regulating your legal status in terms of employment. So what does this permission mean, as you say? I'll put the question to you directly: Did it mean that your employment in Yugoslavia was still in suspension while you were carrying out this new duty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the same conditions as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You agreed to become Mr. Milan Martic's advisor. You say you didn't know him before you became foreign minister of RSK. You got to know him during the cabinet sessions and in the course of your activities as foreign minister. What was your attitude toward him as a person, and what led you to accept his invitation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Martic is an unusually honourable man. He never used his office to get rich, to gain privileges, and he never expressed hatred towards any ethnic or religious group. And those were my own personal standpoints as well, so we got on really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this what led you to accept the post of his advisor for foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to be put in charge of one of the embassies of the FRY, but the situation in which part of the Serb people found themselves in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina did not permit me to put my own personal career ahead of the needs of my imperiled people. I know that I may not be the most capable person, but I knew that I had contacts in all countries of the world which I had acquired as foreign minister, and someone else would have required at least six months to establish these contacts and cooperation. To clarify, let me tell you that as foreign minister I had about 70 volunteers, both Serbs and foreigners, distributing our documents from America to Russia; in France, England, the Netherlands, Australia, almost all important countries of the world. In such circumstances, I could not reject the president's invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last date we mentioned, Mr. Jarcevic, was the 29th of April, 1994, when the Zagreb agreement was signed. However, life had to go on. What were your further activities? Did you have any problems in your new position as advisor to the president of the republic in connection with Bosnia and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, and this is symptomatic for the Balkans, one ethnic group easily falls out with another, or one religious group with another, or one political party with another political party, and of course this always had something to do with the interests of the great powers in Europe and neighbouring Asia. Something that had never happened before happened now. The Muslim community divided into two political camps and fell out with each other. This happened in the so-called Bihac area where the Chamber should know in 1941 the Croatian army slaughtered or threw into pits 16 and a half thousand Orthodox Serbs. So that this territory in the most recent war was mainly inhabited by Muslims, with some Catholics and Orthodox there. About 45.000 people were expelled from their homes by Alija Izetbegovic's army. He was the president of the Croatian Muslim Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was then that Mr. Martic - President Martic - demonstrated the nobility of his character, because these Muslims wanted to go to Croatia across the territory of the RSK, thinking that Croatia was their ally. However, the Croatian army brought heavy weapons, pointed their machine-guns, and did not let them leave Krajina and go to Croatia. In this difficult situation where the RSK was isolated and where the Republic of Yugoslavia was undergoing sanctions, we had to look after 45.000 people in the RSK. They had to be clothed, fed, provided with heating. President Martic issued the order that all reserves of the RSK be directed to the Kordun area in the RSK where these people were now arriving. And if any aid should arrive, if Hungarians and others should let some aid through our borders, the aid should be sent to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you mentioned 45.000 Muslims from the so-called Bihac pocket. Is this area also referred to as the Cazin Krajina? Is that the area you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Cazin Krajina, because this Muslim political group refused to be part of the Muslim and Croatian Bosnia-Herzegovina headed by Alija Izetbegovic. They declared their own republic under the name you have mentioned, the Cazinska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us whether Alija Izetbegovic's army, the army of the Muslim president of the Bosnian Croatian confederation, expelled their own Muslim population because they were disobedient? Is this what it was about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what we've said, you in your question and I in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it under orders of Mr. Martic that these people received assistance? Did they actually receive assistance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. His orders were fully complied with, and thanks to that, those people survived. They were even given every kind of medical assistance. We have doctors who came from France or England, and they can testify to the care with which the medical staff of the Krajina did everything in their power to prevent an epidemic and to treat every ill to the best of their ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, after the Zagreb agreement, which envisaged the separation of military forces at a safe distance, did the political negotiations continue about a solution to the political situation, and when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In June, 1994, a representative of Great Britain turned up. Now the British proposed that they would provide us with peace if we agreed to have secret negotiations with the Croats in London or near London. The proposal was made by a humanitarian organisation. The man at its head was called Smith. I can't recall his first name. He was in charge of a school at a humanitarian organisation in Britain and the message was passed on to us through some Serbs who were citizens of Great Britain, and we were told that this was done in agreement with the Foreign Ministry of Great Britain. As the proposal landed on my desk, I informed the president, Mr. Milan Martic, about it. He approved immediately and said that I should go to attend the negotiations with Croatia and he would inform the cabinet and the cabinet would agree that I go to London for these negotiations. I consulted the ambassador of Great Britain in Belgrade. He consulted his ministry, and he said he would give me a visa to travel to Great Britain, and informed me that the Croatian delegation would also travel there. Just before I left, the British told me that the Croats were hesitating but that the Foreign Ministry of Her Majesty would do everything in their power to encourage the Croats to send their delegation. So it came about that I went to London, and I was accommodated in a castle called Cromwell's castle, about 60 miles away from London. I can't recall the name of the place now, but probably there's someone from Britain here who would know. Something like Hupton [phoen]. Anyway, I waited there for five days for the Croatian delegation to arrive and it failed to turn up. I was received in the British Foreign Ministry. In my book there is a letter which I sent, thanking them for their hospitality, and I asked whether they would do anything to at least reprimand the government and president of Croatia, but they didn't answer my question. They said they were sorry that on this occasion the attempt to have two delegations meet secretly in Great Britain had failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, the so-called Zagreb agreement of the 29th of March, 1994, was an agreement on cessation of hostilities and separation of military forces. Therefore, it was a military agreement. Now, after June, 1994, were there any more attempts to normalise relations and to avoid war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. It is curious that in this agreement that we were supposed to talk about in the UK the British were very specific. It was no longer so generally worded as previous ones, leaving it to commissions to do all the work later. In this agreement formulated by the British, it was exactly formulated who would have which ministry, how they would function together, et cetera. I published all these documents in my book. So maybe, maybe if the Croats had agreed to it - and maybe that's the reason why they didn't agree to it - this agreement would have been binding because it envisaged in detail the steps that were to be taken by the Croat side and the Serb side, and the departments were strictly divided between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, there is written evidence that in November and early December, 1994, some economic agreements were reached. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not participate in those talks. They were handled by the government of Mr. Mikulic. The minister of foreign affairs was then Dr. Milan Babic, and the third minister in line was Mr. Vojinovic. But I know that this motorway between Krajina and Croatia was very pompously opened and Mr. Rade Tanjga, who was the minister on the Croatian side, and he was also the rector of the university, in Krajina he used that motorway to travel to Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you now talking about the implementation of the agreement to normalise economic relations in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Every new agreement relied on the previous one that was signed, and this one relied on the Zagreb agreement which was supposed to be the starting point for all future agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of January, 1995, a plan called Z-4 was referred to. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Our intelligence service was efficient, just as it was in Norway earlier. From New York we received a draft of the agreement that was to be brought later by the American ambassador, Mr. Galbraith, and I sent it to Mr. Martic before the American ambassador brought it to Knin. I was astonished to see that it was the same plan that the Croats had offered us several times in 1992 before I became member of the cabinet. Then they offered it again in January in New York, and then again in March, April, May in Geneva, and after Erdut they stopped putting it on the table. That was followed by the attempt in London and the Zagreb agreement. And it came up again through the American ambassador, the only difference from the previous ones being that it was now mysteriously named Z-4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was Z-4 supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it meant Zagreb. One of the honest British diplomats, whose name eludes me at the moment, frequently warned us of what was being prepared in resolutions against Krajina, and he warned us on this occasion that a plan would be proposed, a very unfavourable plan for Serbs in Krajina, but he advised us to negotiate nevertheless because we would find ourselves in the limelight, and that would give us an opportunity to show who we really are and say the things we wanted to say. He told us, "You will have the opportunity to say that you had statehood back under Austria and that you decided to join the state of Yugoslavia of your own will."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did this plan offer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I told you. We received it from New York. One of the Americans gave it to one of our men, and it was passed on to us. I told you I was astonished because I saw it was the same plan that the Croats had offered us four times; autonomy only in Knin in Glina districts. All the other areas, that is two-thirds of the territory of Croatia, would be automatically included in Croatia without any particular rights for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding that Knin and Glina districts that you mention, this Z-4 plan, what did the plan envisage for these districts? Did it offer any advantages, any privileges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. This was one of the major attempts to trip up the Serbs in Krajina, one of the greatest deceptions. It was wrapped very nicely. It said that Krajina would have its ministries, its president, its money, its customs, its coat of arms and representatives in the bodies of Croatia. It was very enticing, and it is mainly these features that papers in Serbia and Montenegro wrote about. And because of this deception, everybody blamed Krajina Serbs, saying that despite all these good conditions, they didn't want to sign it. However, nobody said that all these things applied only to two districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say they applied to only two districts, can you tell us how many municipalities they encompassed, what part of Krajina's territory; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was one-third of the territory. I've already mentioned this today. One-third of the territory but less than one-third of the population, because the eastern part, that was supposed to be automatically included in Croatia, namely Western Slavonia, was the most densely populated. So it was 11 municipalities around those two towns, whereas Croat municipalities, after 1991, were much smaller than Croat municipalities in the common state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question without leading to any conclusions: Did you find this plan extremely unfavourable to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was not only unfavourable. It was the insolence of offering this plan for the fourth or the fifth time with such awful conditions and presenting it as the salvation of Serbian people. I still wonder at the United Nations and how they dared to offer this plan to the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Martic's approach to the plan the same as yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was much more torn than even I was, and I could only guess, as somebody who knew the situation of our state and our people, but Mr. Martic was in a very difficult situation in those days because President Tudjman was at that time threatening to deny the United Nations force the right to remain in the territory of Croatia, and Mr. Stoltenberg, one of the chairmen of the Conference on Yugoslavia, told Mr. Martic and me in Belgrade that the status of the UN force in Krajina would change and it would no longer be a protection force. And suddenly the president was facing the fact that Croatia would longer treat Krajina even formally as a territory enjoying the protection of an international organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In these proceedings so far we have heard witnesses who spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry. Before you go on, I would like to deal with an area. You have said that Mr. Martic was more torn than you were. You did not speak specifically as to being torn. You said how you felt in relation to the rehash plan, but what is it that Mr. Martic did or said at the time concerning the relevant plan, why you speak of him having been torn? I'm not understanding you here. Please explain further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand that you did not understand me because very few people understand the situation as it was at that time. Mr. Martic was the head of a state, a state that had suffered for a very long time, that had lost its population because it wasn't possible to live under the sanctions, and most families were only looking for a way to save their own lives. Many had moved to Serbia. Many had left for third countries. Compared to 1991, I think the population of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was halved. It was unable to resist Croatia, either militarily or economically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but the specific question that learned counsel Mr. Milovancevic had asked you was how Mr. Martic approached the plan. So what he was trying to elicit from you is from your understanding, observing Mr. Martic at the time, how did he respond to the plan? How did he approach it? And I think you could get to the meat of the question in a more direct way. If you could try for us, because this is important. So please try to get it on the transcript and give the evidence accordingly. We're dealing with Mr. Martic and his approach to the plan. You have mentioned the fact that he was torn. That is a starting point, but you need to tell us how he related to the plan, how he perceived it, how he reacted to it, and the evidence concerning him beyond you and beyond the historic circumstances. We understand that. Please do continue to give us what we need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very simple. Mr. Martic or, rather, President Martic was facing the fact that UN troops would no longer be a protection force. He begged the American ambassador that the plan be placed on the agenda only after the Security Council extends the mandate of the UN Protection Force as envisaged by the Vance Plan. He begged him not to negotiate before that but only after the United Nations confirm what the Vance Plan envisaged, and that's where a clash occurred. This proposal of President Martic was interpreted maliciously and erroneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say that because this plan should not have been proposed in the first place, because it had been proposed four times before that; in 1992 in Knin, in New York in February 1993, on three subsequent occasions over three months in Geneva. So it was the fifth time now that the American ambassador was proposing it, and it included very humiliating conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you have explained right now in response to a question from the Judge that the United Nations Protection Force was running out of time because its mandate was expiring. Was it ever extended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that this was at the request of the Croatian authorities. The term of deployment of the UNPROFOR was always for six months renewable, and after each six months, the Croatian authorities exerted pressure that the UN troops should leave. It was maybe at the insistence of Croatia or maybe because it was in the interest of some Member States, around that time, the mandate of the UN troops was changed and they were no longer a protection force. They became UNCRO, U-N-C-R-O, instead of UNPROFOR, some sort of confidence restoration force, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just told us that Mr. Martic asked the American ambassador Mr. Galbraith not to discussion the plan until the term of the UN force was extended, and you said his request was later maliciously and wrongly interpreted. By whom, can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: All media, both in Yugoslavia and abroad, qualified this as the pigheadedness of Krajina Serbs, and nobody ever mentioned that all these negotiations that we had had previously to which Krajina Serbs had readily agreed had ended in failure because the Croat side never wanted to sign anything. It was interpreted all over the world in that way, and heads of state and journalists alike write to this day that it was Krajina Serbs who didn't want peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did they want peace?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I believe I have already explained that while answering your previous questions. Can you imagine what it was like when the Croats turned a deaf ear to an invitation from the Foreign Ministry of a country like Great Britain while I waited for them five days over there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer is yes. Martic's rejection to consider the plan before the UN force's mandate was extended, was it a final rejection or was it just pending the resolution of that other issue? I think you've already answered part of that question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Martic was only asking that the mandate of the UN force not be changed. Three sides had already signed the plan, including Krajina, and the president of the Assembly signed on behalf of the Krajina. It was also signed by Yugoslavia. It was quite normal that all three sides had to support the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In March 1995, the UN Security Council issued a new Resolution changing the mandate of the peacekeeping force, but it still stayed. This peacekeeping force still remain in the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Croats told their collocutors in other countries and their own public that this was no longer a force protecting the Serb people, and judging by their name, it really wasn't, which meant that that territory was no longer under the protection of the United Nations. And as I said at the beginning, Croats had placed Serbs outside of the law and now Serbs were outside even of the international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, when this new name, UNCRO, was applied to the UN mission and it took on a new role on the territory of the former protected areas, was the Z-4 plan resurrected? Because now the condition that Mr. Martic had asked for had been fulfilled. So was the plan Z-4 again offered to the Croatian side for evaluation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think you have made a slip. Mr. Martic's request had not been granted. The forces were given a different role. They were no longer protection forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In spite of this, was the plan again on offer or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether the Z-4 plan was ever offered again, but it was used for propaganda purposes against the government and president of the RSK. And the Serbian newspapers were especially prominent in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-March, 1995, when the Zagreb agreement on the separation of forces and cessation of hostilities was in force, the Security Council issued a Resolution -- or decision, rather, on the new name of the forces, the UN forces. Did Croatia then attack this territory, and do you remember when this was in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The signal for the Croats was there now. They no longer had a UN protected area there, and brazenly, on behalf of their embassy in New York and other government bodies, also called the Vance Plan the so-called Vance Plan. We asked UN officers and the Security Council to defend their document from such Croatian attacks, but there was never any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will now move on -- or, rather, go back to 1992. You spoke about the activity of the Croatian armed forces in the Kupres area. The armed forces of Croatia were active in the Kupres area on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You explained this was in April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were Croatian forces active in other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a precedent nowhere to be found. The armed forces of Croatia, which had formally been recognised first by the Vatican and then by Germany, made an incursion onto the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the north near Bosanski Brod and, from the south-west, towards Kupres municipality, where I was born. These were regular Croatian forces with tanks, artillery, and all kinds of weapons. As I said at the outset, we who had worked actively on looking after the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina had foreseen this attack, and we had managed to get many Serbs away from the area. However, Serb civilians suffered greatly. For example, the Croatian forces raped Serb girls before the eyes of their parents, and then slaughtered them. This was once shown on Belgrade television and then never again. There was a well-known massacre in the village of Sijekovac and other places, and then the Croatian forces cut off the road to Posavina so that parts of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina were left isolated and desperate. They were isolated by Croatian aggressive forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the cutting off of communications in Bosanska Posavina, are you referring to the area commonly referred to as the so-called corridor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know. This term "corridor" has come into use as if it was on somebody else's territory, but Posavina is inhabited by Serbs, and they are in the majority there, although they suffered in greatly in World War II, and the Serbs from that area and from Mount Kozara, on the border of Posavina, were killed in the concentration death camp of Jasenovac established pursuant to Croatian laws from 1941 when Serbs, Roma, and Gypsies were placed outside the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that Croatian regular units crossed over, abandoning the territory of Croatia which had already been recognised by some countries, and entered the territory of Bosnia and took an area inhabited by a majority Serb population? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it's surprising to note that the United Nations and its members did not condemn Croatia for this aggression. And this was the flywheel of later massacres. It was not the Serbs who caused the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as they did not cause it in Croatia either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you became the foreign minister of the RSK in late October, 1992. This indictment mentions the operation called "corridor," and we've already mentioned this area in Northern Bosnia along the border with Croatia. In this area did Croatian forces later conduct operations? And I'm not asking you about someone who only heard about this through the media, but did you have any information about this from the cabinet sessions of Republika Srpska Krajina when you became a member of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: When I became a member of the cabinet, I reviewed the documentation referring to events from 1990 when Croatia was preparing for secession from Yugoslavia and did not want to use the constitutional provisions according to which every republic could leave Yugoslavia. It was a communist constitution. But in no constitution of any democratic country is there such a specific provision for an area to secede from the country. This was made possible for the republics of Yugoslavia. But the Croatian government, because the Serbs were a state-building nation within Croatia, knew they would not get the agreement of the Serb community as provided for by an article in the constitution, because it was required to get the consent of both nations. So the Croats could not get Serbian lands out of Yugoslavia by peaceful means, which is why they started the war and why they started the persecution of Serbs in 1990. As for the corridor in Kupres that you're asking me about, this was only part of this forcible secession from Yugoslavia, taking Serb lands and expelling the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript - and I think this is what you actually said - it says that Croatia could not leave Yugoslavia because they could not get the consent of the Croatian side. Did you mean the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Serb side, because Croatia was a state with two nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that, in order to leave Yugoslavia, Croatia, under the then-valid constitution of Croatia, needed the consent of both the Serbian people and the Croatian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, as well as the agreement of the remaining five republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was much narrower, so before we break for the day, I wanted to ask you from the materials which, as the new foreign minister, you reviewed, and from your participation in cabinet sessions, did you learn what had been happening in the corridor and why the Serb forces were fighting there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, there were horrendous incidents. In Banja Luka 13 babies were born prematurely. Serb women were giving birth prematurely because they were traumatised. These women had been expelled either from Central Bosnia or from Croatian towns, and these 13 babies could not survive unless they were provided with oxygen. And imagine now the Security Council received a request to make possible a plane -- to make it possible for a plane to help those babies, and this was rejected. All the babies but one died then, however, one of those children died this year because its organism was very weak. A friend of mine in Knin had had a kidney transplant. The kidney was donated by his own brother. He had to go to Belgrade to receive medical assistance for this kidney, and he could not go through the corridor, and this kidney rotted and he has now been dependent on dialysis for 15 years. As a minister of foreign affairs, I sent a letter to the Security Council, asking that in front of the UN palace a monument be erected. This would consist of a picture created by one of our artists who painted an angel with the 12 dead babies. And I asked that such tragedies should never happen again. And these were the consequences of the closing of that corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I feel now is a good time to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We will come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. I beg your pardon, 9.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of July, 2006, at 9.20 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
